Michael Agzarian was charged despite internal legal advice that the images were ‘political satire’, court hears Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Police charged an artist who depicted prominent Australians in military uniforms emblazoned with Nazi symbols despite internal legal advice the images were “political satire”, a court has heard. Police dropped the case against Michael Agzarian before the Downing Centre local court on Friday, almost a year after he had been charged with one count of displaying Nazi symbols by a public act without lawful excuse.

Agzarian had displayed a poster on his shopfront window in Wagga Wagga ahead of last year’s federal election. The poster featured his local MP, Michael McCormack, the opposition leader, Peter Dutton, and mining magnates Gina Rinehart and Clive Palmer in the second world war German army uniforms, the court heard. The court had heard the artwork was adapted from an image from the US sitcom Hogan’s Heroes. McCormack, the Nationals MP for Riverina, made the complaint to police about the image. He told Guardian Australia after the charge against Agzarian was withdrawn that he made the report after several others in the community had also complained. Judge Karen Stafford, who oversaw a cost application and awarded Agzarian more than $12,000 in costs, outlined in court the legal advice given to police by their internal legal counsel.

That advice said: “The crimes act does not define what a Nazi symbol is unlike the criminal code. But in our view none of the imagery would come within either the NSW or commonwealth legislation to be considered an offence. It is political satire.” Stafford found the charges were laid with reasonable cause. But she criticised police for taking seven months to withdraw the charge, even after a hearing date was set. The charge carries a maximum penalty of 12 months in prison or an $11,000 fine. Documents tendered in court revealed Agzarian’s lawyer, Nick Hanna, wrote to police in September requesting they withdraw the charges because it was “inevitable that the prosecution will fail to establish that our client knew that the symbols that he was displaying were Nazi symbols”. However, that request was rejected.

Police charged an artist who depicted prominent Australians in military uniforms emblazoned with Nazi symbols despite internal legal advice the images were “political satire”, a court has heard.

Police dropped the case against Michael Agzarian before the Downing Centre local court on Friday, almost a year after he had been charged with one count of displaying Nazi symbols by a public act without lawful excuse.

Agzarian had displayed a poster on his shopfront window in Wagga Wagga ahead of last year’s federal election. The poster featured his local MP, Michael McCormack, the opposition leader, Peter Dutton, and mining magnates Gina Rinehart and Clive Palmer in the second world war German army uniforms, the court heard. The court had heard the artwork was adapted from an image from the US sitcom Hogan’s Heroes.

McCormack, the Nationals MP for Riverina, made the complaint to police about the image. He told Guardian Australia after the charge against Agzarian was withdrawn that he made the report after several others in the community had also complained.

Judge Karen Stafford, who oversaw a cost application and awarded Agzarian more than $12,000 in costs, outlined in court the legal advice given to police by their internal legal counsel.

That advice said: “The crimes act does not define what a Nazi symbol is unlike the criminal code. But in our view none of the imagery would come within either the NSW or commonwealth legislation to be considered an offence. It is political satire.”

Stafford found the charges were laid with reasonable cause. But she criticised police for taking seven months to withdraw the charge, even after a hearing date was set.

The charge carries a maximum penalty of 12 months in prison or an $11,000 fine.

Documents tendered in court revealed Agzarian’s lawyer, Nick Hanna, wrote to police in September requesting they withdraw the charges because it was “inevitable that the prosecution will fail to establish that our client knew that the symbols that he was displaying were Nazi symbols”. However, that request was rejected.

In February, police seized similar posters from Dissent cafe in Canberra. The artwork, by protest artist group Grow Up Art which is not connected to Agzarian, depicted various world leaders including the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanya

payload.title: Poliisi luopui syytteestä australialaistaiteilijaa vastaan
payload.summary: Australiassa poliisi on luopunut jutusta taiteilija Michael Agzariania vastaan. Häntä oli syytetty natsisymbolien julkisesta esittämisestä, vaikka oikeudessa kuultiin poliisin sisäisen oikeudellisen arvion pitäneen kuvia poliittisena satiirina.
payload.content:
Poliisi on luopunut australialaistaiteilija Michael Agzariania vastaan nostetusta jutusta lähes vuosi sen jälkeen, kun häntä oli syytetty natsisymbolien julkisesta esittämisestä ilman laillista perustetta. Downing Centren paikallistuomioistuimessa perjantaina käsitellyssä asiassa kuultiin, että poliisin sisäinen oikeudellinen neuvonta oli jo aiemmin arvioinut kuvien olevan poliittista satiiria eikä rikos.

## Juliste oli esillä Wagga Waggassa

Agzarian oli asettanut julisteen liikkeensä ikkunaan Wagga Waggassa ennen viime vuoden liittovaltion vaaleja. Oikeudessa kuultiin, että julisteessa hänen paikallinen kansanedustajansa Michael McCormack, oppositiojohtaja Peter Dutton sekä kaivosmiljardöörit Gina Rinehart ja Clive Palmer oli kuvattu toisen maailmansodan aikaisissa Saksan armeijan univormuissa.

Oikeuden mukaan teos oli muokattu yhdysvaltalaisen Hogan’s Heroes -komediasarjan kuvasta. Riverinan vaalipiiriä edustava Nationals-puolueen kansanedustaja McCormack teki kuvasta ilmoituksen poliisille. Hän kertoi myöhemmin tehneensä ilmoituksen sen jälkeen, kun myös useat muut paikalliset olivat hänen mukaansa valittaneet julisteesta.

## Sisäinen arvio piti kuvia satiirina

Tuomari Karen Stafford käsitteli asiassa myös kuluhakemusta ja määräsi Agzarianille yli 12 000 dollarin oikeudenkäyntikuluja. Stafford toi oikeudessa esiin poliisin sisäisen lakineuvonnan, jonka mukaan mikään kuvastosta ei näyttänyt täyttävän Uuden Etelä-Walesin tai liittovaltion lainsäädännön mukaista rikosta. Arviossa todettiin, että kyse oli poliittisesta satiirista.

Stafford katsoi, että syytteiden nostamiselle oli ollut perusteltu syy. Hän kuitenkin arvosteli poliisia siitä, että syytteen peruuttaminen kesti seitsemän kuukautta vielä sen jälkeen, kun käsittelypäivä oli asetettu.

Syytteestä olisi voinut seurata enimmillään 12 kuukauden vankeusrangaistus tai 11 000 dollarin sakko. Oikeudessa esitettyjen asiakirjojen mukaan Agzarianin asianajaja Nick Hanna oli jo syyskuussa pyytänyt poliisia luopumaan syytteistä, koska puolustuksen mukaan syyttäjän olisi ollut väistämättä vaikea näyttää toteen, että Agzarian tiesi esittämiensä symbolien olevan natsisymboleja. Pyyntö oli tuolloin hylätty.

Tuomari arvosteli poliisia siitä, että syytteen peruuttaminen kesti seitsemän kuukautta.
